1	# Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
2	
3	**Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Tao Xu, Greg Brockman, Christine McLeavey, Ilya Sutskever**  
4	*OpenAI, San Francisco, CA*
5	
6	arXiv:2212.04356 (December 2022)
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	A central problem in automatic speech recognition (ASR) is that models optimized on a single
13	data distribution perform well on held-out data from that same distribution but fail in real
14	deployment conditions, making far more errors than humans when applied to different acoustic
15	environments, speakers, or recording conditions. We study whether this robustness gap can be
16	closed by a different training recipe: simply scaling weakly supervised pretraining — using
17	noisily labeled internet audio — to 680,000 hours across 96 languages and four speech
18	processing tasks. The resulting model family, called Whisper, uses an encoder-decoder
19	Transformer trained entirely with next-token prediction on audio-transcript pairs collected
20	from the internet. Without any dataset-specific fine-tuning, zero-shot Whisper achieves
21	55.2% average relative error reduction over a comparably performing supervised model when
22	evaluated on 13 out-of-distribution speech benchmarks. The best Whisper model approaches
23	human-level accuracy and robustness on English speech, is competitive with or surpasses prior
24	work on speech-to-English translation and multilingual recognition, and outperforms commercial
25	ASR services on most long-form transcription benchmarks. Performance degrades on low-resource
26	languages and language identification, and fine-tuning was not studied. Models and inference
27	code are publicly released. {C002}{C003}{C004}
28	
29	---
30	
31	## 1. Introduction
32	
33	### 1.1 The In-Distribution Trap
34	
35	In 2015, Deep Speech 2 (Amodei et al., 2015) reported human-level speech recognition on
36	the LibriSpeech benchmark — clean audiobook recordings. Seven years later, the state-of-the-art
37	word error rate (WER) on that benchmark had fallen another 73%, from 5.3% to 1.4% (Zhang et
38	al., 2021), far below the reported human error rate of 5.8%. These improvements are
39	extraordinary. Yet they do not translate: models trained on LibriSpeech still make far more
40	errors than humans when evaluated on conversational telephone speech, noisy pub environments,
41	African American Vernacular English, or earnings call recordings. {C001}
42	
43	Word error rate, the standard metric in ASR, measures string edit distance between a model's
44	output and a reference transcript. A model that achieves "superhuman" WER on a benchmark may
45	still commit basic errors that a human would never make, precisely because it has learned
46	dataset-specific patterns — formatting conventions, speaker name templates, silence
47	distributions — that happen to reduce WER on held-out data from the *same* source distribution
48	without reflecting genuine understanding of speech (Geirhos et al., 2020). The gap between
49	in-distribution WER and human performance on other distributions is the core problem this
50	paper addresses. {C001}
51	
52	### 1.2 Why Current Approaches Fall Short
53	
54	The dominant paradigm for high-performance ASR combines unsupervised or self-supervised
55	audio pretraining with dataset-specific supervised fine-tuning. Models such as wav2vec 2.0
56	(Baevski et al., 2020) learn powerful audio representations from up to 1,000,000 hours of
57	unlabeled speech (Zhang et al., 2021). These representations are impressive, but the model
58	produces no usable transcript on its own: a supervised decoder must be learned for each
59	deployment distribution via fine-tuning. This fine-tuning step reintroduces the very
60	distributional specificity that pretraining was meant to avoid — a fine-tuned decoder is
61	adept at finding patterns in the target dataset's transcripts that boost evaluation scores
62	without necessarily improving generalization. {C001}
63	
64	An alternative line of work trains entirely supervised models across many datasets
65	simultaneously, demonstrating higher robustness as a result (Narayanan et al., 2018;
66	Likhomanenko et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2021). The largest such effort, SpeechStew
67	(Chan et al., 2021), combines seven datasets totalling 5,140 hours. While a step in the
68	right direction, 5,140 hours is small by modern data standards — comparable to the labeled
69	data used in many image-recognition baselines — and the gain in distributional coverage
70	is limited by what is available at high quality.
71	
72	In computer vision, a closely analogous problem was addressed by scaling weakly supervised
73	pretraining far beyond available high-quality labeled datasets. Training on billions of
74	noisily labeled internet images dramatically improved model robustness and zero-shot
75	transfer (Mahajan et al., 2018; Kolesnikov et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2021). The central
76	question of this paper is whether the same strategy — large-scale weak supervision from
77	internet data — can close the robustness gap for speech recognition.
78	
79	### 1.3 This Work
80	
81	This paper presents Whisper, a speech recognition system trained on 680,000 hours of
82	audio paired with transcripts collected from the internet. This is approximately two orders
83	of magnitude more labeled data than prior multi-domain supervised approaches to speech
84	recognition and an order of magnitude more than prior weakly supervised efforts (Chen et al.,
85	2021; Galvez et al., 2021). We train Whisper entirely with supervised objectives —
86	predicting the next token in a transcript — with no self-supervised or self-training
87	auxiliary losses. {C002}
88	
89	Beyond scale, Whisper is trained to perform multiple speech processing tasks within a single
90	model: multilingual transcription across 96 languages, speech-to-English translation, voice
91	activity detection, and spoken language identification. All tasks are specified through a
92	small set of special tokens prepended to the decoder, allowing a single encoder-decoder
93	Transformer to replace what would traditionally be several separate pipeline components.
94	{C005}
95	
96	We evaluate Whisper entirely in a zero-shot setting — without using any training data from
97	the evaluation benchmarks — across 25+ academic datasets spanning diverse acoustic
98	conditions, languages, and tasks. Our main finding is that this training strategy produces
99	models that generalize across distributions far more effectively than supervised models
100	optimized for a single reference distribution. {C003}
101	
102	---
103	
104	## 2. Background
105	
106	### 2.1 Automatic Speech Recognition and Word Error Rate
107	
108	Automatic speech recognition converts spoken audio into a text transcript. The dominant
109	evaluation metric, word error rate (WER), measures how many word substitutions, deletions,
110	and insertions are needed to transform a model's output into the reference transcript,
111	divided by the number of reference words:
112	
113	> WER = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / Reference words × 100%
114	
115	WER is sensitive to formatting conventions: whether numbers are spelled out, whether
116	contractions are expanded, whether punctuation is present. A model that writes "sixty-eight
117	million dollars" where a reference writes "$68 million" incurs word errors despite conveying
118	identical information. This creates an evaluation challenge for models that were not
119	fine-tuned on a specific dataset's formatting conventions, a particular concern for the
120	zero-shot evaluation in this work. The authors address this through careful text
121	normalization before WER calculation.
122	
123	### 2.2 The Robustness Gap in ASR
124	
125	Taori et al. (2020) formalized the concept of *effective robustness* for image classifiers:
126	how much better (or worse) a model performs on out-of-distribution data *relative to* its
127	in-distribution performance. A model with high effective robustness performs on par with
128	expectations given its in-distribution ability; one with low effective robustness degrades
129	faster than expected when the distribution shifts.
130	
131	The same framing applies to ASR. LibriSpeech — clean audiobook recordings — serves as the
132	community's reference distribution, partly because many models are publicly available with
133	known LibriSpeech WERs. This allows measuring effective robustness directly: given a model's
134	LibriSpeech WER, how does it perform on other benchmarks? As this paper shows, supervised
135	LibriSpeech models have low effective robustness: they perform well on their home benchmark
136	but far worse than humans on diverse real-world benchmarks.
137	
138	### 2.3 Weak Supervision via Internet Data
139	
140	"Weak supervision" in this context means using transcripts that were not produced by paid
141	human annotators working under controlled quality conditions, but were instead collected
142	from the internet — closed captions, user-contributed subtitles, automatically generated
143	captions. Such data is abundant but noisy. Some transcripts are machine-generated (from other
144	ASR systems), misaligned with the audio, or in the wrong language. The key hypothesis,
145	borrowed from the computer vision literature, is that the diversity and scale of internet
146	data outweigh its lower per-example quality for learning robust, generalizable representations.
147	
148	---
149	
150	## 3. Method
151	
152	### 3.1 Training Data
153	
154	The Whisper training dataset consists of 680,000 hours of audio paired with corresponding
155	transcripts, collected from the internet. The dataset is intentionally diverse: it spans
156	many recording environments, speaking styles, languages, and acoustic conditions. Of the
157	total, 438,218 hours cover English speech recognition, 117,113 hours cover multilingual
158	speech recognition in 96 non-English languages, and 125,739 hours cover audio-to-English
159	speech translation tasks. {E001}
160	
161	A key challenge with internet-sourced transcripts is quality. Many are generated by other
162	ASR systems rather than human transcribers; research has shown that training on such
163	"transcript-ese" degrades translation model quality (Ghorbani et al., 2021). To mitigate
164	this, the authors developed heuristics to detect and discard machine-generated transcripts,
165	exploiting signals such as absence of complex punctuation, all-uppercase or all-lowercase
166	formatting, and the absence of contractions. A prototype Whisper model was used in a second
167	filtering pass to identify and manually inspect training data sources with anomalously high
168	error rates. Language detection was applied to ensure that audio and transcript languages
169	match, with mismatched pairs redirected to the translation training set when the transcript
170	is in English. Transcript-level fuzzy deduplication was applied, and overlap with key
171	evaluation datasets was removed. {E028}
172	
173	Audio files were segmented into 30-second chunks paired with the corresponding portion of
174	the transcript. All audio was resampled to 16,000 Hz.
175	
176	### 3.2 Model Architecture
177	
178	Whisper uses an encoder-decoder Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), the same architecture
179	class widely used in sequence-to-sequence tasks in NLP and translation. The choice of
180	architecture was deliberate: the authors aimed to study the effect of large-scale pretraining,
181	not architectural innovations. Five model sizes were trained:
182	
183	| Size   | Parameters | Layers | Width | Heads |
184	|--------|-----------|--------|-------|-------|
185	| Tiny   | 39 M      | 4      | 384   | 6     |
186	| Base   | 74 M      | 6      | 512   | 8     |
187	| Small  | 244 M     | 12     | 768   | 12    |
188	| Medium | 769 M     | 24     | 1,024 | 16    |
189	| Large  | 1,550 M   | 32     | 1,280 | 20    |
190	
191	The audio encoder takes as input an 80-channel log-magnitude Mel spectrogram computed on
192	25 ms windows with a 10 ms stride — a standard acoustic feature representation that converts
193	the raw audio waveform into a time-frequency representation. Two convolutional layers with
194	GELU activations compress the spectrogram before Transformer blocks with sinusoidal position
195	embeddings process it. The decoder uses learned position embeddings and ties its input and
196	output token embeddings.
197	
198	The text tokenizer is the byte-level BPE tokenizer from GPT-2 (Sennrich et al., 2015;
199	Radford et al., 2019) for English-only models, with the vocabulary refitted for multilingual
200	models to avoid fragmentation of non-English scripts. {E002}
201	
202	### 3.3 Multitask Training Format
203	
204	The decoder is conditioned on a sequence of special tokens that specify the task before
205	generating the transcript. The token sequence is:
206	
207	1. `<|startoftranscript|>` — marks the beginning of decoding
208	2. A language token (one of 99 language tags, sourced from a language detection model
209	   trained on VoxLingua107) — identifies which language is spoken
210	3. A task token — `<|transcribe|>` for ASR or `<|translate|>` for speech-to-English translation
211	4. A timestamp/no-timestamp token — `<|notimestamps|>` or the beginning of time-aligned output
212	5. Optionally, a `<|nospeech|>` token — for voice activity detection output
213	
214	This format means that voice activity detection, language identification, transcription, and
215	translation are all expressed as conditional token prediction over a shared vocabulary —
216	the same forward pass handles all four tasks by changing only the conditioning tokens. With
217	some probability during training, the transcript of the preceding audio segment is also
218	prepended to the decoder input, allowing the model to use longer-range text context. {E003}
219	
220	### 3.4 Training Details
221	
222	Models were trained with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) and gradient norm clipping
223	(Pascanu et al., 2013), with a linear learning rate decay to zero after 2,048 warmup steps.
224	A batch size of 256 audio segments and 2^20 total update steps were used, corresponding to
225	two to three passes over the full dataset. Because the training set is so large and so few
226	epochs are used, overfitting was not a concern, and no data augmentation or regularization
227	was applied. All models were trained in mixed precision (FP16). {E029}
228	
229	An improved variant, Large V2, was trained for 2.5 times more update steps with SpecAugment
230	(Park et al., 2019), Stochastic Depth (Huang et al., 2016), and BPE Dropout (Provilkov et
231	al., 2019) added for regularization. Reported results for the Large model refer to Large V2
232	unless otherwise noted. {E030}
233	
234	---
235	
236	## 4. Results
237	
238	All Whisper evaluations are performed in a *zero-shot* setting: no training data from any
239	evaluation benchmark is used at any point. Standard text normalization is applied before
240	WER computation to avoid penalizing the model for formatting differences rather than
241	genuine transcription errors.
242	
243	### 4.1 English Speech Recognition: The Robustness Test
244	
245	The central experimental question is whether zero-shot Whisper, trained on diverse internet
246	data, generalizes better across distributions than supervised models trained specifically on
247	a curated English ASR dataset. LibriSpeech serves as the reference benchmark, because (a) many
248	publicly released supervised models use it as their training set, and (b) its WER provides a
249	common scale for measuring effective robustness. {C001}
250	
251	The comparison partner is wav2vec 2.0 Large (no language model), a state-of-the-art
252	supervised baseline that achieves 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean. The best zero-shot
253	Whisper model (Large V2, beam search with temperature fallback) also achieves 2.7% WER on
254	LibriSpeech test-clean — the two models are effectively matched on their common reference
255	distribution. {E004}
256	
257	The critical result is what happens on 13 other academic ASR datasets spanning
258	conversational speech (Switchboard, CallHome), spontaneous telephone calls (CORAAL),
259	noisy multi-speaker recordings (CHiME-6, AMI), read sentences with accent variation
260	(Artie bias corpus), podcasts (Common Voice), political speech (VoxPopuli), and others.
261	On these datasets, zero-shot Whisper achieves a **55.2% average relative error reduction**
262	over the supervised baseline. {C003}{E005}
263	
264	| Dataset       | wav2vec 2.0 Large (WER%) | Whisper Large V2 (WER%) | Relative Error Reduction |
265	|---------------|--------------------------|-------------------------|--------------------------|
266	| LibriSpeech (clean) | 2.7 | 2.7 | 0% (reference) |
267	| Artie        | 24.5 | 6.2 | 74.7% |
268	| Common Voice | 29.9 | 9.0 | 69.9% |
269	| CHiME-6      | 65.8 | 25.5 | 61.2% |
270	| CORAAL       | 35.6 | 16.2 | 54.5% |
271	| AMI (IHM)    | 37.0 | 16.9 | 54.3% |
272	| Switchboard  | 28.3 | 13.8 | 51.2% |
273	| CallHome     | 34.8 | 17.6 | 49.4% |
274	| WSJ          | 7.7  | 3.9  | 49.4% |
275	| AMI (SDM1)   | 67.6 | 36.4 | 46.2% |
276	| LibriSpeech (other) | 6.2 | 5.2 | 16.1% |
277	| **Average**  | 29.3 | 12.8 | **55.2%** |
278	
279	*Table: Effective robustness comparison. Whisper and the supervised baseline are matched at 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean; on 13 other datasets, Whisper achieves 55.2% average relative error reduction. Results after text normalization. (Source: Table 2 in Radford et al., 2022.)*
280	
281	This result is striking not only because of its magnitude but because of what it controls for:
282	in-distribution performance is held constant. The 55.2% RER measures *effective robustness*
283	specifically, not raw performance. A model with only 39 million parameters — Whisper Tiny
284	with 6.7% WER on LibriSpeech — is "roughly competitive with the best supervised LibriSpeech
285	model when evaluated on other datasets," the authors note. The robustness advantage thus
286	does not require the largest model; it is a property of diverse training data. {C002}{E007}
287	
288	### 4.2 Comparison with Human Performance
289	
290	To contextualise performance relative to human transcribers, the authors computed a
291	*robustness frontier*: for each zero-shot Whisper model size, they plotted average WER on
292	three out-of-distribution datasets against WER on LibriSpeech. Supervised LibriSpeech
293	models cluster far above this frontier (worse robustness for a given in-distribution WER),
294	while zero-shot Whisper models trace a frontier that includes the 95% confidence interval
295	for a single human evaluator's performance on the same datasets. {C004}{E008}
296	
297	A more direct human comparison was conducted on 25 recordings from the Kincaid46 dataset —
298	a collection of diverse audio including broadcast speech, telephone calls, and meetings —
299	where five professional transcription services provided references. Among the compared
300	services, a computer-assisted human transcription service was the most accurate overall,
301	achieving an aggregate WER 1.15 percentage points lower than Whisper. The four purely human
302	transcription services performed only a fraction of a percentage point better than Whisper.
303	{C009}{E015}
304	
305	These results indicate that Whisper's English ASR performance is not perfect — some
306	irreducible errors remain — but that it has reached the level at which the gap to professional
307	human transcribers is small and, in some conditions, within measurement noise.
308	
309	### 4.3 Multilingual Speech Recognition
310	
311	Whisper was evaluated on two commonly used multilingual benchmarks: Multilingual LibriSpeech
312	(MLS, Pratap et al., 2020b), covering 8 languages, and VoxPopuli (Wang et al., 2021),
313	covering 16 European languages, in zero-shot mode. On MLS, zero-shot Whisper (7.3% WER)
314	outperforms fine-tuned XLS-R (Babu et al., 2021) at 10.9% and is comparable to Maestro
315	(Chen et al., 2022b) at 7.3%. On VoxPopuli, however, Whisper lags substantially behind
316	Maestro (13.6% vs. 8.1% WER), likely because other models use VoxPopuli as a major
317	unsupervised pretraining source and VoxPopuli has substantially more supervised data per
318	language (roughly 10× more than MLS). {E009}{E021}
319	
320	To understand performance across a broader set of languages, the authors evaluated on the
321	Fleurs dataset (Conneau et al., 2022), which covers 102 languages. A strong linear
322	relationship emerges between the log of per-language training data and the log of WER
323	(r² = 0.83), with WER approximately halving for every 16-fold increase in training hours.
324	{C012}{E010} Languages that deviate most from this trend — performing worse than the scaling
325	law predicts — tend to have unique scripts or are linguistically distant from the
326	Indo-European languages that dominate the training set (e.g., Hebrew, Telugu, Chinese, Korean).
327	The training dataset is heavily English-centric due to data collection from English-dominated
328	parts of the internet, with most non-English languages having fewer than 1,000 hours of
329	training data. Performance on low-resource languages remains correspondingly poor. {E025}
330	
331	### 4.4 Speech-to-English Translation
332	
333	On the CoVoST 2 benchmark (Wang et al., 2020b), which tests translation from 21 source
334	languages into English, zero-shot Whisper achieves 29.1 BLEU overall — a new state of the
335	art among compared models, improving over mSLAM-CTC (24.8) and Maestro (25.2). The
336	advantage is most pronounced on low-resource languages: on the lowest-resource language
337	group, Whisper improves over mSLAM by 6.7 BLEU, a gain the authors attribute to the much
338	larger (68,000 hours) translation training data in the Whisper dataset compared to 861 hours
339	in CoVoST2's training split. On high-resource languages, Whisper (36.2 BLEU) does not
340	improve over Maestro (38.2) or mSLAM (37.8), where abundant supervised fine-tuning data
341	gives those models an advantage. The authors caution that the text standardizer used in this
342	comparison was developed alongside Whisper, preventing confident SOTA claims. {C010}{E011}{E022}
343	
344	### 4.5 Language Identification
345	
346	Zero-shot Whisper achieves 64.5% language identification accuracy on Fleurs, substantially
347	below the supervised state of the art (mSLAM-CTC: 77.7%). However, this comparison is
348	confounded: Whisper has no training data for 20 of the 102 Fleurs languages, capping its
349	theoretically achievable accuracy at 80.4%. On the 82 languages where Whisper has training
350	data, it achieves 80.3% — within 0.1% of the theoretical maximum. Language identification is
351	therefore a structural limitation of the current training data rather than a fundamental
352	failure of the approach. {C013}{E012}{E020}
353	
354	### 4.6 Long-form Transcription
355	
356	Whisper's 30-second context window requires a buffered transcription strategy for audio
357	longer than 30 seconds: consecutive segments are transcribed, with the window shifted
358	according to predicted timestamps. This introduces failure modes including repetition loops
359	and hallucination. The authors developed a set of decoding heuristics to address these:
360	beam search (5 beams) instead of greedy decoding, temperature fallback when outputs are
361	implausibly repetitive or have low log-probability, voice activity detection to skip silent
362	segments, and previous-text conditioning for continuity. These heuristics reduce average WER
363	across 7 long-form datasets from 11.0% (greedy only) to 10.0% (full heuristic stack). {E019}
364	
365	On these seven long-form benchmarks — ranging from TED talks and podcasts to earnings calls
366	and interviews — Whisper outperforms all compared open-source ASR models and performs better
367	than commercial ASR services on most benchmarks. The authors note that some commercial
368	services may have trained on these publicly available datasets, making the comparison
369	approximate. {C011}{E014}
370	
371	---
372	
373	## 5. Analysis and Ablations
374	
375	### 5.1 Model Scale
376	
377	Performance improves with model size across all tasks except English speech recognition,
378	which shows diminishing returns at the larger model sizes. The authors interpret this
379	saturation as consistent with approaching human-level performance on English ASR specifically
380	— where further gains from scale are constrained by irreducible errors in the data rather
381	than model capacity. For multilingual recognition, translation, and language identification,
382	scaling continues to improve results from 39 M to 1,550 M parameters. {C006}{E016}
383	
384	### 5.2 Dataset Scale
385	
386	A medium-sized Whisper model was trained on subsets ranging from 0.5% to 100% of the full
387	680,000-hour dataset to measure data scaling effects. All three tasks improve monotonically
388	with data:
389	
390	| Dataset Size (hours) | English WER (↓) | Multilingual WER (↓) | X→En BLEU (↑) |
391	|---------------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------|
392	| 3,405               | 30.5            | 92.4                | 0.2           |
393	| 6,811               | 19.6            | 72.7                | 1.7           |
394	| 13,621              | 14.4            | 56.6                | 7.9           |
395	| 27,243              | 12.3            | 45.0                | 13.9          |
396	| 54,486              | 10.9            | 36.4                | 19.2          |
397	| 681,070             | 9.9             | 29.2                | 24.8          |
398	
399	*Table: Performance vs. dataset size for a medium-sized Whisper model. All metrics improve monotonically; translation BLEU is near zero at 7,000 hours or fewer. (Source: Table 6 in Radford et al., 2022.)*
400	
401	{C007}{E017}
402	
403	English WER improves rapidly from 3,000 to 13,000 hours then slows noticeably, again
404	consistent with approaching a human-level saturation regime. Multilingual WER follows a
405	power-law trend through 54,000 hours. Translation BLEU is near zero below 7,000 hours — a
406	minimum-data threshold effect — then follows a roughly log-linear trend. At the largest
407	scale (54,000 to 680,000 hours), all three tasks show diminishing returns, which the authors
408	interpret as either under-training relative to dataset size or a genuine plateau in
409	data-scaling benefits for speech recognition.
410	
411	### 5.3 Multitask and Multilingual Transfer
412	
413	Joint training on multiple tasks and languages means the model is learning many things
414	simultaneously. A natural concern is *negative transfer*: interference between tasks that
415	degrades performance on each individual task compared to a task-specific model. To test this,
416	the authors compared English-only models with jointly trained models at equal compute budgets
417	adjusted for the fraction of compute devoted to English SR (about 65% in joint training).
418	
419	At small model sizes and limited compute, joint training does hurt English SR — negative
420	transfer is real. However, as model size and compute increase, joint models improve faster
421	and eventually surpass English-only models. At the largest experiments, joint training yields
422	positive transfer, with jointly trained models even slightly outperforming English-only
423	models without any compute adjustment. This suggests that exposure to diverse speech during
424	training improves the model's general acoustic representations in ways that benefit even
425	English-only tasks, but only when the model is large enough to learn both without interference.
426	{C008}{E018}
427	
428	### 5.4 Noise Robustness
429	
430	Whisper was tested under additive white noise and pub noise (ambient restaurant/pub sounds)
431	across a range of signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), alongside 14 other ASR models including
432	multiple variants of wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, and NVIDIA STT conformer models. Under low noise
433	(40 dB SNR), many compared models outperform Whisper — unsurprising given that those models
434	are trained on clean LibriSpeech-style data. Under high noise (SNR below 10 dB), all 14
435	compared models perform worse than Whisper under pub noise, demonstrating a consistent
436	robustness advantage in challenging acoustic conditions. {E013}
437	
438	### 5.5 Text Normalization
439	
440	A concern with the evaluation methodology is that the text normalizer used to compute WER
441	was developed alongside Whisper models, potentially inflating Whisper's apparent advantage
442	by discounting formatting errors that Whisper makes more often than other models. To check
443	this, the authors compared their normalizer against the independently developed FairSpeech
444	normalizer (Koenecke et al., 2020). On most benchmarks, the two normalizers produce similar
445	relative WER differences between Whisper and other models. On three benchmarks — WSJ,
446	CallHome, and Switchboard — Whisper benefits noticeably more from the authors' normalizer,
447	due to specific formatting conventions (number expressions, contractions) that the authors'
448	normalizer handles more permissively. This indicates a modest evaluation bias on those
449	specific benchmarks, which the authors acknowledge. {E027}{L004}
450	
451	---
452	
453	## 6. Discussion
454	
455	### 6.1 Distributional Coverage as the Driver of Robustness
456	
457	The central empirical finding — that a zero-shot model trained on diverse weakly labeled
458	internet data substantially outperforms a supervised model matched on an in-distribution
459	benchmark — supports a specific hypothesis about what drives the robustness gap in ASR.
460	
461	Models trained on a single dataset distribution do not simply fail to *see* the variety of
462	accents, noise conditions, and speaking styles in the real world. They actively exploit
463	dataset-specific patterns — formatting idiosyncrasies, recording equipment signatures,
464	sentence length distributions, vocabulary distributions specific to the source — that reliably
465	predict reference transcript tokens but do not generalize. This is a concrete manifestation
466	of "shortcut learning" (Geirhos et al., 2020): the model solves the right problem on the
467	training distribution but learns the wrong solution. {C001}
468	
469	Whisper's training distribution covers an enormous range of acoustic conditions, languages,
470	domains, and recording environments. The diversity acts as a regularizer: no single
471	distributional quirk consistently predicts transcript tokens across 680,000 hours of diverse
472	internet audio. The model must therefore learn representations that are robust to those
473	variations. The 55.2% average relative error reduction over the supervised baseline is the
474	empirical measure of how much benefit that distributional breadth provides. {C003}
475	
476	### 6.2 Reframing the 'Superhuman' Label
477	
478	A recurring narrative in ASR research is that models have achieved "superhuman" performance
479	on LibriSpeech. The paper's authors argue, and the data support, that this label is
480	misleading. The comparison between a human transcriber and a machine model is confounded
481	by a fundamental difference in their training: the human is evaluated without any prior
482	exposure to LibriSpeech-style audio, while the machine is evaluated after training
483	extensively on it. A human performing a task with no distributional training is being tested
484	for out-of-distribution generalization; a machine trained on the distribution is being
485	tested for in-distribution generalization. {C001}
486	
487	This confounding makes machine-versus-human WER comparisons on any single benchmark
488	uninformative about whether machines are better at speech recognition in general. What is
489	informative is the comparison across *multiple* distributions, as in Figure 2 of the paper:
490	zero-shot Whisper models approach human *robustness* not because they are better at
491	LibriSpeech specifically, but because they generalize across distributions in a way that
492	matches how humans — who are never trained on a specific benchmark distribution — generalize.
493	{C004}
494	
495	### 6.3 Connection to Weak Supervision at Scale in Other Domains
496	
497	Whisper's approach is directly analogous to how large-scale weak supervision was used
498	in computer vision. Models trained on billions of noisily labeled internet images, such as
499	CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and BiT (Kolesnikov et al., 2020), showed dramatically improved
500	zero-shot transfer to diverse downstream tasks. The success of this approach in vision
501	motivated the hypothesis that it would transfer to audio, and the results support that
502	hypothesis. The key enabling factor in both cases is that internet-scale data is diverse
503	enough that learning to predict the weak labels requires learning something close to genuine
504	semantic understanding of the content, rather than dataset-specific shortcuts.
505	
506	### 6.4 Limitations
507	
508	Several important limitations constrain how broadly these results can be interpreted.
509	
510	**Fine-tuning not evaluated.** The entire paper focuses on zero-shot transfer, which is the
511	most stringent and general-purpose setting. For many practical deployments where labeled
512	in-domain data is available, fine-tuning Whisper could yield substantially better performance
513	than the zero-shot numbers reported here. This remains unstudied. {L003}
514	
515	**Low-resource language performance.** Most non-English languages have fewer than 1,000 hours
516	of training data in the Whisper dataset, due to the English-centric nature of the internet
517	sources from which data was collected. The scaling law (r² = 0.83, WER halves per 16× data
518	increase) makes clear that improving these languages would require targeted data collection —
519	a straightforward path but one not yet taken. {E025}{L010}
520	
521	**Long-form decoding failures.** While the heuristic decoding strategy substantially improves
522	long-form transcription, failure modes including hallucination and repetition loops remain.
523	These are characteristic of sequence-to-sequence generation with attention and are not
524	fully solved by the beam search and temperature fallback described. {E024}
525	
526	**Evaluation fairness.** The text normalizer was developed jointly with Whisper, introducing
527	modest evaluation bias on some benchmarks. The comparison with commercial ASR services is
528	imperfect because some commercial systems may have been trained on the evaluation datasets.
529	The human comparison uses a small sample (25 recordings) without reported confidence
530	intervals. {L004}{L005}
531	
532	**Language identification.** Whisper's language identification performance is significantly
533	below the supervised state of the art on the full Fleurs benchmark, though much of this gap
534	is a direct consequence of missing training data for 20 of 102 languages rather than a
535	representational failure. {L006}
536	
537	---
538	
539	## 7. Related Work
540	
541	### 7.1 Scaling Supervised and Semi-supervised ASR
542	
543	A consistent thread in ASR research over the past decade is that scale — of models, data,
544	and compute — reliably improves performance. Deep Speech 2 (Amodei et al., 2015) demonstrated
545	high-throughput distributed training across 16 GPUs at 12,000 hours. Narayanan et al. (2018)
546	used semi-supervised pre-training to scale to 162,000 hours of labeled audio. BigSSL (Zhang
547	et al., 2021) pushed unsupervised pretraining to 1,000,000 hours and supervised fine-tuning
548	to multi-billion-parameter models. Whisper occupies a distinct point in this space: 680,000
549	hours of *supervised* (though weakly labeled) data, without the unsupervised pretraining
550	stage.
551	
552	### 7.2 Self-supervised and Unsupervised Speech Pretraining
553	
554	wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020) demonstrated that self-supervised contrastive learning on
555	unlabeled audio could learn speech representations competitive with supervised baselines when
556	fine-tuned. HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021a) improved on this with masked prediction of
557	pseudo-labels. XLS-R (Babu et al., 2021) scaled multilingual self-supervised pretraining.
558	These models share an important property: the pretrained encoder alone is not an ASR system
559	— a supervised decoder must be learned separately. Whisper's end-to-end training sidesteps
560	this requirement.
561	
562	### 7.3 Multitask Learning for Speech
563	
564	Multitask learning for speech recognition has a long history. Toshniwal et al. (2018) jointly
565	trained a deep learning ASR model on multiple languages. Pratap et al. (2020a) scaled this
566	to 50 languages with a billion-parameter model. mSLAM (Bapna et al., 2022) extended joint
567	pretraining to both speech and text. The innovation in Whisper's approach is expressing all
568	tasks through a token-based conditioning format that requires no architectural changes and
569	allows a single decoder to cover the full task space.
570	
571	### 7.4 Robustness and Distribution Shift in Machine Learning
572	
573	The robustness of machine learning models to distribution shift has been studied across
574	vision (Taori et al., 2020), NLP (Hendrycks et al., 2020), and question answering (Miller
575	et al., 2020). A recurring finding is that multi-domain training consistently improves
576	robustness — a finding that Whisper confirms for speech at an unprecedented scale. The
577	parallel to CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), which showed that natural language supervision at
578	scale produced zero-shot visual classification competitive with supervised models, is direct:
579	both works demonstrate that sufficiently large and diverse weakly supervised training can
580	match task-specific supervised performance while far surpassing it in out-of-distribution
581	settings.
582	
583	---
584	
585	## 8. Conclusion
586	
587	Whisper demonstrates that the robustness gap between human and machine speech recognition
588	is not primarily a fundamental capability gap, but a training distribution gap. A single
589	encoder-decoder Transformer trained on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised internet audio —
590	without any self-supervised pretraining, without any dataset-specific fine-tuning, and
591	without any data augmentation — achieves 55.2% average relative error reduction over a
592	comparable supervised model on 13 diverse out-of-distribution benchmarks, approaches human
593	accuracy on English speech, reaches state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on speech
594	translation, and outperforms commercial ASR systems on most long-form transcription tasks.
595	{C002}{C003}{C004}
596	
597	The result suggests that scaling weakly supervised pretraining in speech has been
598	underappreciated relative to the unsupervised pretraining paradigm that has dominated recent
599	large-scale ASR work. Diverse, noisily labeled data at sufficient scale appears to produce
600	the same distributional breadth that humans implicitly develop from a lifetime of exposure
601	to varied speech — and that breadth, not in-distribution specialization, is what produces
602	robust, human-like generalization.
603	
604	Key limitations remain: performance on most non-English languages is constrained by limited
605	training data, fine-tuning has not been studied, and long-form transcription has known
606	failure modes. Targeted data collection for low-resource languages, decoding improvements
607	for long audio, and fine-tuning studies represent the most direct paths forward.
608	
609	---
610	
611	## References

# Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision

**Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Tao Xu, Greg Brockman, Christine McLeavey, Ilya Sutskever**  
*OpenAI, San Francisco, CA*

arXiv:2212.04356 (December 2022)

---

## Abstract

A central problem in automatic speech recognition (ASR) is that models optimized on a single
data distribution perform well on held-out data from that same distribution but fail in real
deployment conditions, making far more errors than humans when applied to different acoustic
environments, speakers, or recording conditions. We study whether this robustness gap can be
closed by a different training recipe: simply scaling weakly supervised pretraining — using
noisily labeled internet audio — to 680,000 hours across 96 languages and four speech
processing tasks. The resulting model family, called Whisper, uses an encoder-decoder
Transformer trained entirely with next-token prediction on audio-transcript pairs collected
from the internet. Without any dataset-specific fine-tuning, zero-shot Whisper achieves
55.2% average relative error reduction over a comparably performing supervised model when
evaluated on 13 out-of-distribution speech benchmarks. The best Whisper model approaches
human-level accuracy and robustness on English speech, is competitive with or surpasses prior
work on speech-to-English translation and multilingual recognition, and outperforms commercial
ASR services on most long-form transcription benchmarks. Performance degrades on low-resource
languages and language identification, and fine-tuning was not studied. Models and inference
code are publicly released. {C002}{C003}{C004}

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 The In-Distribution Trap

In 2015, Deep Speech 2 (Amodei et al., 2015) reported human-level speech recognition on
the LibriSpeech benchmark — clean audiobook recordings. Seven years later, the state-of-the-art
word error rate (WER) on that benchmark had fallen another 73%, from 5.3% to 1.4% (Zhang et
al., 2021), far below the reported human error rate of 5.8%. These improvements are
extraordinary. Yet they do not translate: models trained on LibriSpeech still make far more
errors than humans when evaluated on conversational telephone speech, noisy pub environments,
African American Vernacular English, or earnings call recordings. {C001}

Word error rate, the standard metric in ASR, measures string edit distance between a model's
output and a reference transcript. A model that achieves "superhuman" WER on a benchmark may
still commit basic errors that a human would never make, precisely because it has learned
dataset-specific patterns — formatting conventions, speaker name templates, silence
distributions — that happen to reduce WER on held-out data from the *same* source distribution
without reflecting genuine understanding of speech (Geirhos et al., 2020). The gap between
in-distribution WER and human performance on other distributions is the core problem this
paper addresses. {C001}

### 1.2 Why Current Approaches Fall Short

The dominant paradigm for high-performance ASR combines unsupervised or self-supervised
audio pretraining with dataset-specific supervised fine-tuning. Models such as wav2vec 2.0
(Baevski et al., 2020) learn powerful audio representations from up to 1,000,000 hours of
unlabeled speech (Zhang et al., 2021). These representations are impressive, but the model
produces no usable transcript on its own: a supervised decoder must be learned for each
deployment distribution via fine-tuning. This fine-tuning step reintroduces the very
distributional specificity that pretraining was meant to avoid — a fine-tuned decoder is
adept at finding patterns in the target dataset's transcripts that boost evaluation scores
without necessarily improving generalization. {C001}

An alternative line of work trains entirely supervised models across many datasets
simultaneously, demonstrating higher robustness as a result (Narayanan et al., 2018;
Likhomanenko et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2021). The largest such effort, SpeechStew
(Chan et al., 2021), combines seven datasets totalling 5,140 hours. While a step in the
right direction, 5,140 hours is small by modern data standards — comparable to the labeled
data used in many image-recognition baselines — and the gain in distributional coverage
is limited by what is available at high quality.

In computer vision, a closely analogous problem was addressed by scaling weakly supervised
pretraining far beyond available high-quality labeled datasets. Training on billions of
noisily labeled internet images dramatically improved model robustness and zero-shot
transfer (Mahajan et al., 2018; Kolesnikov et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2021). The central
question of this paper is whether the same strategy — large-scale weak supervision from
internet data — can close the robustness gap for speech recognition.

### 1.3 This Work

This paper presents Whisper, a speech recognition system trained on 680,000 hours of
audio paired with transcripts collected from the internet. This is approximately two orders
of magnitude more labeled data than prior multi-domain supervised approaches to speech
recognition and an order of magnitude more than prior weakly supervised efforts (Chen et al.,
2021; Galvez et al., 2021). We train Whisper entirely with supervised objectives —
predicting the next token in a transcript — with no self-supervised or self-training
auxiliary losses. {C002}

Beyond scale, Whisper is trained to perform multiple speech processing tasks within a single
model: multilingual transcription across 96 languages, speech-to-English translation, voice
activity detection, and spoken language identification. All tasks are specified through a
small set of special tokens prepended to the decoder, allowing a single encoder-decoder
Transformer to replace what would traditionally be several separate pipeline components.
{C005}

We evaluate Whisper entirely in a zero-shot setting — without using any training data from
the evaluation benchmarks — across 25+ academic datasets spanning diverse acoustic
conditions, languages, and tasks. Our main finding is that this training strategy produces
models that generalize across distributions far more effectively than supervised models
optimized for a single reference distribution. {C003}

## 2. Background

### 2.1 Automatic Speech Recognition and Word Error Rate

Automatic speech recognition converts spoken audio into a text transcript. The dominant
evaluation metric, word error rate (WER), measures how many word substitutions, deletions,
and insertions are needed to transform a model's output into the reference transcript,
divided by the number of reference words:

> WER = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / Reference words × 100%

WER is sensitive to formatting conventions: whether numbers are spelled out, whether
contractions are expanded, whether punctuation is present. A model that writes "sixty-eight
million dollars" where a reference writes "$68 million" incurs word errors despite conveying
identical information. This creates an evaluation challenge for models that were not
fine-tuned on a specific dataset's formatting conventions, a particular concern for the
zero-shot evaluation in this work. The authors address this through careful text
normalization before WER calculation.

### 2.2 The Robustness Gap in ASR

Taori et al. (2020) formalized the concept of *effective robustness* for image classifiers:
how much better (or worse) a model performs on out-of-distribution data *relative to* its
in-distribution performance. A model with high effective robustness performs on par with
expectations given its in-distribution ability; one with low effective robustness degrades
faster than expected when the distribution shifts.

The same framing applies to ASR. LibriSpeech — clean audiobook recordings — serves as the
community's reference distribution, partly because many models are publicly available with
known LibriSpeech WERs. This allows measuring effective robustness directly: given a model's
LibriSpeech WER, how does it perform on other benchmarks? As this paper shows, supervised
LibriSpeech models have low effective robustness: they perform well on their home benchmark
but far worse than humans on diverse real-world benchmarks.

### 2.3 Weak Supervision via Internet Data

"Weak supervision" in this context means using transcripts that were not produced by paid
human annotators working under controlled quality conditions, but were instead collected
from the internet — closed captions, user-contributed subtitles, automatically generated
captions. Such data is abundant but noisy. Some transcripts are machine-generated (from other
ASR systems), misaligned with the audio, or in the wrong language. The key hypothesis,
borrowed from the computer vision literature, is that the diversity and scale of internet
data outweigh its lower per-example quality for learning robust, generalizable representations.

## 3. Method

### 3.1 Training Data

The Whisper training dataset consists of 680,000 hours of audio paired with corresponding
transcripts, collected from the internet. The dataset is intentionally diverse: it spans
many recording environments, speaking styles, languages, and acoustic conditions. Of the
total, 438,218 hours cover English speech recognition, 117,113 hours cover multilingual
speech recognition in 96 non-English languages, and 125,739 hours cover audio-to-English
speech translation tasks. {E001}

A key challenge with internet-sourced transcripts is quality. Many are generated by other
ASR systems rather than human transcribers; research has shown that training on such
"transcript-ese" degrades translation model quality (Ghorbani et al., 2021). To mitigate
this, the authors developed heuristics to detect and discard machine-generated transcripts,
exploiting signals such as absence of complex punctuation, all-uppercase or all-lowercase
formatting, and the absence of contractions. A prototype Whisper model was used in a second
filtering pass to identify and manually inspect training data sources with anomalously high
error rates. Language detection was applied to ensure that audio and transcript languages
match, with mismatched pairs redirected to the translation training set when the transcript
is in English. Transcript-level fuzzy deduplication was applied, and overlap with key
evaluation datasets was removed. {E028}

Audio files were segmented into 30-second chunks paired with the corresponding portion of
the transcript. All audio was resampled to 16,000 Hz.

### 3.2 Model Architecture

Whisper uses an encoder-decoder Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), the same architecture
class widely used in sequence-to-sequence tasks in NLP and translation. The choice of
architecture was deliberate: the authors aimed to study the effect of large-scale pretraining,
not architectural innovations. Five model sizes were trained:

| Size   | Parameters | Layers | Width | Heads |
|--------|-----------|--------|-------|-------|
| Tiny   | 39 M      | 4      | 384   | 6     |
| Base   | 74 M      | 6      | 512   | 8     |
| Small  | 244 M     | 12     | 768   | 12    |
| Medium | 769 M     | 24     | 1,024 | 16    |
| Large  | 1,550 M   | 32     | 1,280 | 20    |

The audio encoder takes as input an 80-channel log-magnitude Mel spectrogram computed on
25 ms windows with a 10 ms stride — a standard acoustic feature representation that converts
the raw audio waveform into a time-frequency representation. Two convolutional layers with
GELU activations compress the spectrogram before Transformer blocks with sinusoidal position
embeddings process it. The decoder uses learned position embeddings and ties its input and
output token embeddings.

The text tokenizer is the byte-level BPE tokenizer from GPT-2 (Sennrich et al., 2015;
Radford et al., 2019) for English-only models, with the vocabulary refitted for multilingual
models to avoid fragmentation of non-English scripts. {E002}

### 3.3 Multitask Training Format

The decoder is conditioned on a sequence of special tokens that specify the task before
generating the transcript. The token sequence is:

1. `<|startoftranscript|>` — marks the beginning of decoding
2. A language token (one of 99 language tags, sourced from a language detection model
   trained on VoxLingua107) — identifies which language is spoken
3. A task token — `<|transcribe|>` for ASR or `<|translate|>` for speech-to-English translation
4. A timestamp/no-timestamp token — `<|notimestamps|>` or the beginning of time-aligned output
5. Optionally, a `<|nospeech|>` token — for voice activity detection output

This format means that voice activity detection, language identification, transcription, and
translation are all expressed as conditional token prediction over a shared vocabulary —
the same forward pass handles all four tasks by changing only the conditioning tokens. With
some probability during training, the transcript of the preceding audio segment is also
prepended to the decoder input, allowing the model to use longer-range text context. {E003}

### 3.4 Training Details

Models were trained with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) and gradient norm clipping
(Pascanu et al., 2013), with a linear learning rate decay to zero after 2,048 warmup steps.
A batch size of 256 audio segments and 2^20 total update steps were used, corresponding to
two to three passes over the full dataset. Because the training set is so large and so few
epochs are used, overfitting was not a concern, and no data augmentation or regularization
was applied. All models were trained in mixed precision (FP16). {E029}

An improved variant, Large V2, was trained for 2.5 times more update steps with SpecAugment
(Park et al., 2019), Stochastic Depth (Huang et al., 2016), and BPE Dropout (Provilkov et
al., 2019) added for regularization. Reported results for the Large model refer to Large V2
unless otherwise noted. {E030}

## 4. Results

All Whisper evaluations are performed in a *zero-shot* setting: no training data from any
evaluation benchmark is used at any point. Standard text normalization is applied before
WER computation to avoid penalizing the model for formatting differences rather than
genuine transcription errors.

### 4.1 English Speech Recognition: The Robustness Test

The central experimental question is whether zero-shot Whisper, trained on diverse internet
data, generalizes better across distributions than supervised models trained specifically on
a curated English ASR dataset. LibriSpeech serves as the reference benchmark, because (a) many
publicly released supervised models use it as their training set, and (b) its WER provides a
common scale for measuring effective robustness. {C001}

The comparison partner is wav2vec 2.0 Large (no language model), a state-of-the-art
supervised baseline that achieves 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean. The best zero-shot
Whisper model (Large V2, beam search with temperature fallback) also achieves 2.7% WER on
LibriSpeech test-clean — the two models are effectively matched on their common reference
distribution. {E004}

The critical result is what happens on 13 other academic ASR datasets spanning
conversational speech (Switchboard, CallHome), spontaneous telephone calls (CORAAL),
noisy multi-speaker recordings (CHiME-6, AMI), read sentences with accent variation
(Artie bias corpus), podcasts (Common Voice), political speech (VoxPopuli), and others.
On these datasets, zero-shot Whisper achieves a **55.2% average relative error reduction**
over the supervised baseline. {C003}{E005}

| Dataset       | wav2vec 2.0 Large (WER%) | Whisper Large V2 (WER%) | Relative Error Reduction |
|---------------|--------------------------|-------------------------|--------------------------|
| LibriSpeech (clean) | 2.7 | 2.7 | 0% (reference) |
| Artie        | 24.5 | 6.2 | 74.7% |
| Common Voice | 29.9 | 9.0 | 69.9% |
| CHiME-6      | 65.8 | 25.5 | 61.2% |
| CORAAL       | 35.6 | 16.2 | 54.5% |
| AMI (IHM)    | 37.0 | 16.9 | 54.3% |
| Switchboard  | 28.3 | 13.8 | 51.2% |
| CallHome     | 34.8 | 17.6 | 49.4% |
| WSJ          | 7.7  | 3.9  | 49.4% |
| AMI (SDM1)   | 67.6 | 36.4 | 46.2% |
| LibriSpeech (other) | 6.2 | 5.2 | 16.1% |
| **Average**  | 29.3 | 12.8 | **55.2%** |

*Table: Effective robustness comparison. Whisper and the supervised baseline are matched at 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean; on 13 other datasets, Whisper achieves 55.2% average relative error reduction. Results after text normalization. (Source: Table 2 in Radford et al., 2022.)*

This result is striking not only because of its magnitude but because of what it controls for:
in-distribution performance is held constant. The 55.2% RER measures *effective robustness*
specifically, not raw performance. A model with only 39 million parameters — Whisper Tiny
with 6.7% WER on LibriSpeech — is "roughly competitive with the best supervised LibriSpeech
model when evaluated on other datasets," the authors note. The robustness advantage thus
does not require the largest model; it is a property of diverse training data. {C002}{E007}

### 4.2 Comparison with Human Performance

To contextualise performance relative to human transcribers, the authors computed a
*robustness frontier*: for each zero-shot Whisper model size, they plotted average WER on
three out-of-distribution datasets against WER on LibriSpeech. Supervised LibriSpeech
models cluster far above this frontier (worse robustness for a given in-distribution WER),
while zero-shot Whisper models trace a frontier that includes the 95% confidence interval
for a single human evaluator's performance on the same datasets. {C004}{E008}

A more direct human comparison was conducted on 25 recordings from the Kincaid46 dataset —
a collection of diverse audio including broadcast speech, telephone calls, and meetings —
where five professional transcription services provided references. Among the compared
services, a computer-assisted human transcription service was the most accurate overall,
achieving an aggregate WER 1.15 percentage points lower than Whisper. The four purely human
transcription services performed only a fraction of a percentage point better than Whisper.
{C009}{E015}

These results indicate that Whisper's English ASR performance is not perfect — some
irreducible errors remain — but that it has reached the level at which the gap to professional
human transcribers is small and, in some conditions, within measurement noise.

### 4.3 Multilingual Speech Recognition

Whisper was evaluated on two commonly used multilingual benchmarks: Multilingual LibriSpeech
(MLS, Pratap et al., 2020b), covering 8 languages, and VoxPopuli (Wang et al., 2021),
covering 16 European languages, in zero-shot mode. On MLS, zero-shot Whisper (7.3% WER)
outperforms fine-tuned XLS-R (Babu et al., 2021) at 10.9% and is comparable to Maestro
(Chen et al., 2022b) at 7.3%. On VoxPopuli, however, Whisper lags substantially behind
Maestro (13.6% vs. 8.1% WER), likely because other models use VoxPopuli as a major
unsupervised pretraining source and VoxPopuli has substantially more supervised data per
language (roughly 10× more than MLS). {E009}{E021}

To understand performance across a broader set of languages, the authors evaluated on the
Fleurs dataset (Conneau et al., 2022), which covers 102 languages. A strong linear
relationship emerges between the log of per-language training data and the log of WER
(r² = 0.83), with WER approximately halving for every 16-fold increase in training hours.
{C012}{E010} Languages that deviate most from this trend — performing worse than the scaling
law predicts — tend to have unique scripts or are linguistically distant from the
Indo-European languages that dominate the training set (e.g., Hebrew, Telugu, Chinese, Korean).
The training dataset is heavily English-centric due to data collection from English-dominated
parts of the internet, with most non-English languages having fewer than 1,000 hours of
training data. Performance on low-resource languages remains correspondingly poor. {E025}

### 4.4 Speech-to-English Translation

On the CoVoST 2 benchmark (Wang et al., 2020b), which tests translation from 21 source
languages into English, zero-shot Whisper achieves 29.1 BLEU overall — a new state of the
art among compared models, improving over mSLAM-CTC (24.8) and Maestro (25.2). The
advantage is most pronounced on low-resource languages: on the lowest-resource language
group, Whisper improves over mSLAM by 6.7 BLEU, a gain the authors attribute to the much
larger (68,000 hours) translation training data in the Whisper dataset compared to 861 hours
in CoVoST2's training split. On high-resource languages, Whisper (36.2 BLEU) does not
improve over Maestro (38.2) or mSLAM (37.8), where abundant supervised fine-tuning data
gives those models an advantage. The authors caution that the text standardizer used in this
comparison was developed alongside Whisper, preventing confident SOTA claims. {C010}{E011}{E022}

### 4.5 Language Identification

Zero-shot Whisper achieves 64.5% language identification accuracy on Fleurs, substantially
below the supervised state of the art (mSLAM-CTC: 77.7%). However, this comparison is
confounded: Whisper has no training data for 20 of the 102 Fleurs languages, capping its
theoretically achievable accuracy at 80.4%. On the 82 languages where Whisper has training
data, it achieves 80.3% — within 0.1% of the theoretical maximum. Language identification is
therefore a structural limitation of the current training data rather than a fundamental
failure of the approach. {C013}{E012}{E020}

### 4.6 Long-form Transcription

Whisper's 30-second context window requires a buffered transcription strategy for audio
longer than 30 seconds: consecutive segments are transcribed, with the window shifted
according to predicted timestamps. This introduces failure modes including repetition loops
and hallucination. The authors developed a set of decoding heuristics to address these:
beam search (5 beams) instead of greedy decoding, temperature fallback when outputs are
implausibly repetitive or have low log-probability, voice activity detection to skip silent
segments, and previous-text conditioning for continuity. These heuristics reduce average WER
across 7 long-form datasets from 11.0% (greedy only) to 10.0% (full heuristic stack). {E019}

On these seven long-form benchmarks — ranging from TED talks and podcasts to earnings calls
and interviews — Whisper outperforms all compared open-source ASR models and performs better
than commercial ASR services on most benchmarks. The authors note that some commercial
services may have trained on these publicly available datasets, making the comparison
approximate. {C011}{E014}

## 5. Analysis and Ablations

### 5.1 Model Scale

Performance improves with model size across all tasks except English speech recognition,
which shows diminishing returns at the larger model sizes. The authors interpret this
saturation as consistent with approaching human-level performance on English ASR specifically
— where further gains from scale are constrained by irreducible errors in the data rather
than model capacity. For multilingual recognition, translation, and language identification,
scaling continues to improve results from 39 M to 1,550 M parameters. {C006}{E016}

### 5.2 Dataset Scale

A medium-sized Whisper model was trained on subsets ranging from 0.5% to 100% of the full
680,000-hour dataset to measure data scaling effects. All three tasks improve monotonically
with data:

| Dataset Size (hours) | English WER (↓) | Multilingual WER (↓) | X→En BLEU (↑) |
|---------------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------|
| 3,405               | 30.5            | 92.4                | 0.2           |
| 6,811               | 19.6            | 72.7                | 1.7           |
| 13,621              | 14.4            | 56.6                | 7.9           |
| 27,243              | 12.3            | 45.0                | 13.9          |
| 54,486              | 10.9            | 36.4                | 19.2          |
| 681,070             | 9.9             | 29.2                | 24.8          |

*Table: Performance vs. dataset size for a medium-sized Whisper model. All metrics improve monotonically; translation BLEU is near zero at 7,000 hours or fewer. (Source: Table 6 in Radford et al., 2022.)*

{C007}{E017}

English WER improves rapidly from 3,000 to 13,000 hours then slows noticeably, again
consistent with approaching a human-level saturation regime. Multilingual WER follows a
power-law trend through 54,000 hours. Translation BLEU is near zero below 7,000 hours — a
minimum-data threshold effect — then follows a roughly log-linear trend. At the largest
scale (54,000 to 680,000 hours), all three tasks show diminishing returns, which the authors
interpret as either under-training relative to dataset size or a genuine plateau in
data-scaling benefits for speech recognition.

### 5.3 Multitask and Multilingual Transfer

Joint training on multiple tasks and languages means the model is learning many things
simultaneously. A natural concern is *negative transfer*: interference between tasks that
degrades performance on each individual task compared to a task-specific model. To test this,
the authors compared English-only models with jointly trained models at equal compute budgets
adjusted for the fraction of compute devoted to English SR (about 65% in joint training).

At small model sizes and limited compute, joint training does hurt English SR — negative
transfer is real. However, as model size and compute increase, joint models improve faster
and eventually surpass English-only models. At the largest experiments, joint training yields
positive transfer, with jointly trained models even slightly outperforming English-only
models without any compute adjustment. This suggests that exposure to diverse speech during
training improves the model's general acoustic representations in ways that benefit even
English-only tasks, but only when the model is large enough to learn both without interference.
{C008}{E018}

### 5.4 Noise Robustness

Whisper was tested under additive white noise and pub noise (ambient restaurant/pub sounds)
across a range of signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), alongside 14 other ASR models including
multiple variants of wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, and NVIDIA STT conformer models. Under low noise
(40 dB SNR), many compared models outperform Whisper — unsurprising given that those models
are trained on clean LibriSpeech-style data. Under high noise (SNR below 10 dB), all 14
compared models perform worse than Whisper under pub noise, demonstrating a consistent
robustness advantage in challenging acoustic conditions. {E013}

### 5.5 Text Normalization

A concern with the evaluation methodology is that the text normalizer used to compute WER
was developed alongside Whisper models, potentially inflating Whisper's apparent advantage
by discounting formatting errors that Whisper makes more often than other models. To check
this, the authors compared their normalizer against the independently developed FairSpeech
normalizer (Koenecke et al., 2020). On most benchmarks, the two normalizers produce similar
relative WER differences between Whisper and other models. On three benchmarks — WSJ,
CallHome, and Switchboard — Whisper benefits noticeably more from the authors' normalizer,
due to specific formatting conventions (number expressions, contractions) that the authors'
normalizer handles more permissively. This indicates a modest evaluation bias on those
specific benchmarks, which the authors acknowledge. {E027}{L004}

## 6. Discussion

### 6.1 Distributional Coverage as the Driver of Robustness

The central empirical finding — that a zero-shot model trained on diverse weakly labeled
internet data substantially outperforms a supervised model matched on an in-distribution
benchmark — supports a specific hypothesis about what drives the robustness gap in ASR.

Models trained on a single dataset distribution do not simply fail to *see* the variety of
accents, noise conditions, and speaking styles in the real world. They actively exploit
dataset-specific patterns — formatting idiosyncrasies, recording equipment signatures,
sentence length distributions, vocabulary distributions specific to the source — that reliably
predict reference transcript tokens but do not generalize. This is a concrete manifestation
of "shortcut learning" (Geirhos et al., 2020): the model solves the right problem on the
training distribution but learns the wrong solution. {C001}

Whisper's training distribution covers an enormous range of acoustic conditions, languages,
domains, and recording environments. The diversity acts as a regularizer: no single
distributional quirk consistently predicts transcript tokens across 680,000 hours of diverse
internet audio. The model must therefore learn representations that are robust to those
variations. The 55.2% average relative error reduction over the supervised baseline is the
empirical measure of how much benefit that distributional breadth provides. {C003}

### 6.2 Reframing the 'Superhuman' Label

A recurring narrative in ASR research is that models have achieved "superhuman" performance
on LibriSpeech. The paper's authors argue, and the data support, that this label is
misleading. The comparison between a human transcriber and a machine model is confounded
by a fundamental difference in their training: the human is evaluated without any prior
exposure to LibriSpeech-style audio, while the machine is evaluated after training
extensively on it. A human performing a task with no distributional training is being tested
for out-of-distribution generalization; a machine trained on the distribution is being
tested for in-distribution generalization. {C001}

This confounding makes machine-versus-human WER comparisons on any single benchmark
uninformative about whether machines are better at speech recognition in general. What is
informative is the comparison across *multiple* distributions, as in Figure 2 of the paper:
zero-shot Whisper models approach human *robustness* not because they are better at
LibriSpeech specifically, but because they generalize across distributions in a way that
matches how humans — who are never trained on a specific benchmark distribution — generalize.
{C004}

### 6.3 Connection to Weak Supervision at Scale in Other Domains

Whisper's approach is directly analogous to how large-scale weak supervision was used
in computer vision. Models trained on billions of noisily labeled internet images, such as
CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and BiT (Kolesnikov et al., 2020), showed dramatically improved
zero-shot transfer to diverse downstream tasks. The success of this approach in vision
motivated the hypothesis that it would transfer to audio, and the results support that
hypothesis. The key enabling factor in both cases is that internet-scale data is diverse
enough that learning to predict the weak labels requires learning something close to genuine
semantic understanding of the content, rather than dataset-specific shortcuts.

### 6.4 Limitations

Several important limitations constrain how broadly these results can be interpreted.

**Fine-tuning not evaluated.** The entire paper focuses on zero-shot transfer, which is the
most stringent and general-purpose setting. For many practical deployments where labeled
in-domain data is available, fine-tuning Whisper could yield substantially better performance
than the zero-shot numbers reported here. This remains unstudied. {L003}

**Low-resource language performance.** Most non-English languages have fewer than 1,000 hours
of training data in the Whisper dataset, due to the English-centric nature of the internet
sources from which data was collected. The scaling law (r² = 0.83, WER halves per 16× data
increase) makes clear that improving these languages would require targeted data collection —
a straightforward path but one not yet taken. {E025}{L010}

**Long-form decoding failures.** While the heuristic decoding strategy substantially improves
long-form transcription, failure modes including hallucination and repetition loops remain.
These are characteristic of sequence-to-sequence generation with attention and are not
fully solved by the beam search and temperature fallback described. {E024}

**Evaluation fairness.** The text normalizer was developed jointly with Whisper, introducing
modest evaluation bias on some benchmarks. The comparison with commercial ASR services is
imperfect because some commercial systems may have been trained on the evaluation datasets.
The human comparison uses a small sample (25 recordings) without reported confidence
intervals. {L004}{L005}

**Language identification.** Whisper's language identification performance is significantly
below the supervised state of the art on the full Fleurs benchmark, though much of this gap
is a direct consequence of missing training data for 20 of 102 languages rather than a
representational failure. {L006}

## 7. Related Work

### 7.1 Scaling Supervised and Semi-supervised ASR

A consistent thread in ASR research over the past decade is that scale — of models, data,
and compute — reliably improves performance. Deep Speech 2 (Amodei et al., 2015) demonstrated
high-throughput distributed training across 16 GPUs at 12,000 hours. Narayanan et al. (2018)
used semi-supervised pre-training to scale to 162,000 hours of labeled audio. BigSSL (Zhang
et al., 2021) pushed unsupervised pretraining to 1,000,000 hours and supervised fine-tuning
to multi-billion-parameter models. Whisper occupies a distinct point in this space: 680,000
hours of *supervised* (though weakly labeled) data, without the unsupervised pretraining
stage.

### 7.2 Self-supervised and Unsupervised Speech Pretraining

wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020) demonstrated that self-supervised contrastive learning on
unlabeled audio could learn speech representations competitive with supervised baselines when
fine-tuned. HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021a) improved on this with masked prediction of
pseudo-labels. XLS-R (Babu et al., 2021) scaled multilingual self-supervised pretraining.
These models share an important property: the pretrained encoder alone is not an ASR system
— a supervised decoder must be learned separately. Whisper's end-to-end training sidesteps
this requirement.

### 7.3 Multitask Learning for Speech

Multitask learning for speech recognition has a long history. Toshniwal et al. (2018) jointly
trained a deep learning ASR model on multiple languages. Pratap et al. (2020a) scaled this
to 50 languages with a billion-parameter model. mSLAM (Bapna et al., 2022) extended joint
pretraining to both speech and text. The innovation in Whisper's approach is expressing all
tasks through a token-based conditioning format that requires no architectural changes and
allows a single decoder to cover the full task space.

### 7.4 Robustness and Distribution Shift in Machine Learning

The robustness of machine learning models to distribution shift has been studied across
vision (Taori et al., 2020), NLP (Hendrycks et al., 2020), and question answering (Miller
et al., 2020). A recurring finding is that multi-domain training consistently improves
robustness — a finding that Whisper confirms for speech at an unprecedented scale. The
parallel to CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), which showed that natural language supervision at
scale produced zero-shot visual classification competitive with supervised models, is direct:
both works demonstrate that sufficiently large and diverse weakly supervised training can
match task-specific supervised performance while far surpassing it in out-of-distribution
settings.

---

## 8. Conclusion

Whisper demonstrates that the robustness gap between human and machine speech recognition
is not primarily a fundamental capability gap, but a training distribution gap. A single
encoder-decoder Transformer trained on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised internet audio —
without any self-supervised pretraining, without any dataset-specific fine-tuning, and
without any data augmentation — achieves 55.2% average relative error reduction over a
comparable supervised model on 13 diverse out-of-distribution benchmarks, approaches human
accuracy on English speech, reaches state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on speech
translation, and outperforms commercial ASR systems on most long-form transcription tasks.
{C002}{C003}{C004}

The result suggests that scaling weakly supervised pretraining in speech has been
underappreciated relative to the unsupervised pretraining paradigm that has dominated recent
large-scale ASR work. Diverse, noisily labeled data at sufficient scale appears to produce
the same distributional breadth that humans implicitly develop from a lifetime of exposure
to varied speech — and that breadth, not in-distribution specialization, is what produces
robust, human-like generalization.

Key limitations remain: performance on most non-English languages is constrained by limited
training data, fine-tuning has not been studied, and long-form transcription has known
failure modes. Targeted data collection for low-resource languages, decoding improvements
for long audio, and fine-tuning studies represent the most direct paths forward.
